claims.text: A eutectic alloy design approach can enable large-scale production of high-entropy alloys.
Eutectic alloy design can produce a stable, fine-lamellar microstructure in refractory high-entropy alloy composites containing Cu.
Eutectic alloy design mitigates problems caused by the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu.
The initial material is a non-eutectic blended mixture of refractory high-entropy alloying elements and Cu or Cu-containing powder.
Controlled solidification of a eutectic composition promotes a eutectic reaction during processing.
Rapid solidification is a suitable example of a processing technique for obtaining the proposed eutectic microstructure.
High-temperature processing under controlled cooling, potentially in an inert atmosphere, fosters simultaneous nucleation of two interpenetrating phases.
Eutectic high-entropy alloys can possess alternating soft fcc and hard bcc or B2 phases in a fine lamellar microstructure.
A eutectic reaction produces a self-organized fine lamellar structure.
The fine lamellar structure minimizes local compositional fluctuations.
The fine lamellar structure reduces segregation caused by the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu.
The proposed lamellar structure stabilizes the composite microstructure.
The eutectic lamellar structure enhances high-temperature mechanical performance.
The eutectic lamellar structure enhances oxidation resistance.
The processed refractory-high-entropy-alloy/Cu composite will have a more uniform and stable lamellar microstructure than a conventionally processed composite.
The eutectically processed composite will have better high-temperature mechanical properties than a conventionally processed composite.
Conventional non-eutectic casting or sintering tends to produce compositional segregation and unstable microstructures in refractory-high-entropy-alloy/Cu composites.
Success depends on attaining a precise eutectic composition and a controlled cooling rate.
Departures from the required composition or cooling rate may form brittle intermetallic compounds or cause phase instability.
The efficacy of eutectic design for the specific refractory-element/Cu mixing problem has not been established and requires systematic validation.
